```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2)
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Robust crossing finder: the naloxone concentration at which `y` first
# crosses `level`, interpolated on log-concentration. Returns NA if the curve
# never crosses, and tolerates repeated/flat values (approx() errors on those).
crossing <- function(x, y, level) {
  o <- order(x)
  x <- x[o]
  y <- y[o]
  below <- y < level
  idx <- which(below[-length(below)] != below[-1])
  if (length(idx) == 0) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }
  i <- idx[1]
  w <- (level - y[i]) / (y[i + 1] - y[i])
  exp(log(x[i]) + w * (log(x[i + 1]) - log(x[i])))
}
```

# Model and source

* Citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Dahan_2026_naloxone"))$reference`
* Description: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Dahan_2026_naloxone"))$description`
* Article: [Front Pharmacol 2026;17:1944044](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphar.2026.1944044)

This is a mechanistic PK/PD *simulation* model, not a data-fitted population PK
model. It couples an established ventilatory PK/PD model of fentanyl-induced
respiratory depression (Boom 2013) with a novel mechanistic model of
naloxone-precipitated opioid withdrawal, and expresses the trade-off between the
two as a utility function. Because the output axis is a steady-state naloxone
concentration rather than a time course, there is no NCA target to validate
against; instead the vignette reproduces the paper's Figures 2-4 and the
analytic crossover relationship of Equation 8.

# Population

No new human data were collected. The model is a Monte-Carlo simulation over
virtual opioid-tolerant adults with an opioid use disorder (OUD) experiencing a
fentanyl overdose that is treated with intravenous naloxone (Dahan 2026,
Methods). Each scenario in the paper drew 40,000 virtual subjects; only the
fentanyl potency C50 varies between subjects (log-normal, variance 0.31), while
all other parameters are held at their typical values because inter-individual
variability could not be estimated from the available data. Parameter values are
literature-sourced (Table 1): the ventilatory model from Boom 2013, the
OUD-specific C50 from Algera 2020, the naloxone inhibition constant from
Moss 2020 / Stolbach 2023, the naloxone effect-site rate constant from
van Lemmen 2025b, and the naloxone volume and elimination rate constant from the
FDA 2022 review. The withdrawal threshold *w* was calibrated against
emergency-department (Yugar 2023) and prospective naloxone (van Lemmen 2025b,
2026) dose-withdrawal data.

The metadata is available programmatically via
`readModelDb("Dahan_2026_naloxone")()$population`.

# Model structure

For a typical subject the fentanyl effect-site concentration `ce_fent` is held
fixed at the value giving the chosen overdose severity `R0` (Equation 4
rearranged, Figure 1):

$$C_E = \frac{R_0}{1-R_0}\,C_{50}.$$

Naloxone is dosed into a one-compartment disposition model (`central`) with a
hysteresis effect compartment (`effect`). The naloxone effect-site concentration
competitively lowers the effective fentanyl concentration at the receptor
(Equation 1):

$$C_{EF} = \frac{C_E}{1 + C_{NALE}/K_i}.$$

`CEF` then drives both the inhibitory sigmoid-Emax ventilation model
(Equations 2-3) and the normalized mu-opioid receptor activation
`R = CEF / (CEF + C50)` (Equation 5). Model-defined respiratory reversal is
`R < 0.5`; precipitated withdrawal is `R < (1 - w) * R0` (Equation 6). The
per-subject `utility` is `reversal - k * withdrawal`; the population utility
(Equation 7) is the cohort mean.

# Source trace

| Equation / parameter | Value | Source location |
|----------------------|-------|-----------------|
| `lvc` (Vd)           | 128 L | Table 1, naloxone Vd (FDA 2022) |
| `lkel` (ke)          | 0.0077 min-1 | Table 1, naloxone ke (FDA 2022) |
| `lke0` (ke0N)        | 0.087 min-1 | Table 1, naloxone ke0 (van Lemmen 2025b) |
| `lkd` (Ki)           | 1.5 ng/mL | Table 1, naloxone Ki (Moss 2020; Stolbach 2023); Equation 1 |
| `le0` (EMAX)         | 19.9 L/min | Table 1, EMAX (Boom 2013); Equation 2 |
| `lec50` (C50)        | 4.08 ng/mL | Methods text (Table 1 rounds to 4.1; Algera 2020) |
| `hill` (gamma)       | 1 | Table 1, gamma (Boom 2013); Equation 3 |
| `rbase` (R0)         | 0.9 | Table 1 range 0-0.97; Figures 3-4 reference value |
| `wd_thres` (w)       | 0.30 | Abstract and Table 1 (95% CI 0.16-0.40); Equation 6 |
| `wd_weight` (k)      | 1 | Table 1 range 0.25-4; Equation 7 reference value |
| `etalec50` (omega2)  | 0.31 | Table 1, omega2(C50), log-domain (Boom 2013) |
| `d/dt(central)`      | n/a | One-compartment naloxone disposition |
| `d/dt(effect)`       | n/a | Effect-compartment hysteresis, Figure 1 (ke0N) |
| `ceff_fent`, `ract`  | n/a | Equations 1, 5 |
| `reversal`, `withdrawal`, `utility` | n/a | Equations 6-7, Figure 1 |

# Virtual cohort and simulation helper

Original observed data are not publicly available. Each scenario uses a virtual
cohort of **200 subjects** whose only varying parameter is the fentanyl potency
C50, drawn on a deterministic log-normal quantile grid (variance 0.31) so the
figures are reproducible on any machine regardless of solver-thread count.

A steady-state naloxone effect-site concentration is imposed on each subject with
a bolus-plus-infusion pair into the `central` compartment: the loading bolus
sets the initial plasma concentration and the matched zero-order infusion holds
it, so after equilibration the effect-site concentration equals the target
`C_NALE`.

```{r helper}
mod <- readModelDb("Dahan_2026_naloxone")
VC <- 128        # L, naloxone Vd
KEL <- 0.0077    # 1/min, naloxone ke

n_sub <- 200L
# Deterministic C50 IIV: log-normal quantiles, variance 0.31 (Table 1).
eta_grid <- qnorm((seq_len(n_sub) - 0.5) / n_sub) * sqrt(0.31)

# Steady-state naloxone effect-site concentration grid (ng/mL), 0.1-300 (Methods).
nale_grid <- 10^seq(-1, log10(300), length.out = 45)

# Build events + params for a data frame of scenarios (columns R0, w, k).
simulate_scenarios <- function(scenarios) {
  grid <- tidyr::expand_grid(scenarios, nale = nale_grid)
  grid$scen <- seq_len(nrow(grid))
  long <- tidyr::expand_grid(grid, sid = seq_len(n_sub))
  long$id <- seq_len(nrow(long))

  # mg giving the target steady-state plasma (hence effect-site) concentration.
  # A loading bolus sets the plasma level and a matched zero-order infusion
  # holds it: with rate = amt_css * KEL the central amount stays at amt_css, so
  # Cc = 1000 * amt_css / VC = nale throughout. The effect site equilibrates in
  # ~5 half-lives of ke0 (t1/2 ~ 8 min); the readout at 500 min is deep inside
  # the infusion window (extended to 1200 min) so it never coincides with the
  # infusion-end discontinuity.
  amt_css <- long$nale * VC / 1000           # ng/mL -> mg in 128 L
  t_obs <- 500
  events <- dplyr::bind_rows(
    data.frame(id = long$id, time = 0, evid = 1, amt = amt_css,
               rate = 0, cmt = "central"),
    data.frame(id = long$id, time = 0, evid = 1,
               amt = amt_css * KEL * 1200, rate = amt_css * KEL,
               cmt = "central"),
    data.frame(id = long$id, time = t_obs, evid = 0, amt = 0,
               rate = 0, cmt = "central")
  ) |>
    dplyr::arrange(id, time, dplyr::desc(evid))

  params <- data.frame(
    id = long$id, etalec50 = eta_grid[long$sid],
    rbase = long$R0, wd_thres = long$w, wd_weight = long$k
  )

  sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, events, params = params, returnType = "data.frame")
  # Keep the equilibrated readout record per subject.
  sim <- sim[sim$time == t_obs, ]
  sim$scen <- long$scen[match(sim$id, long$id)]
  dplyr::left_join(
    dplyr::as_tibble(sim),
    dplyr::select(grid, scen, R0, w, k, nale),
    by = "scen"
  ) |>
    dplyr::group_by(R0, w, k, nale) |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      ventilation = mean(vent),
      receptor_activation = mean(ract),
      p_reversal = mean(reversal),
      p_withdrawal = mean(withdrawal),
      utility = mean(utility),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}
```

# Figure 2a - ventilation versus fentanyl effect-site concentration

With no naloxone present, the effective fentanyl concentration equals the
effect-site concentration, so sweeping the overdose severity `R0` sweeps the
fentanyl concentration `C_E = R0/(1-R0) * C50`. Plotting the typical-subject
ventilation against `C_E` reproduces the inhibitory sigmoid, which crosses 50 %
of baseline (9.95 L/min) at `C_E = C50 = 4.08` ng/mL.

```{r figure-2a}
# The model has no residual error, so zero only the omega (C50 IIV).
mod_typ <- rxode2::zeroRe(mod, which = "omega")
r0_sweep <- seq(0.01, 0.985, length.out = 120)
ce_sweep <- r0_sweep / (1 - r0_sweep) * 4.08
fig2a <- data.frame(id = seq_along(r0_sweep), time = 0, evid = 0,
                    amt = 0, cmt = "central")
f2a <- rxode2::rxSolve(
  mod_typ, fig2a,
  params = data.frame(id = seq_along(r0_sweep), rbase = r0_sweep),
  returnType = "data.frame"
)
f2a$CE <- ce_sweep

ggplot(f2a, aes(CE, vent)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 19.9 / 2, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 4.08, linetype = "dotted") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Fentanyl effect-site concentration (ng/mL)",
       y = "Minute ventilation (L/min)",
       title = "Figure 2a - fentanyl concentration vs minute ventilation",
       caption = "Replicates Figure 2a of Dahan 2026.")

# The sigmoid must cross 50% of baseline at C_E = C50.
ce50 <- crossing(f2a$CE, -f2a$vent, -19.9 / 2)
stopifnot(abs(ce50 - 4.08) < 0.1)
```

# Figure 2b - receptor activation and withdrawal probability versus naloxone

Higher baseline receptor activation `R0` shifts the withdrawal-probability
curves to the right (Figure 2b): a more severe overdose needs a higher naloxone
concentration to reach the same withdrawal probability.

```{r figure-2b}
fig2b <- simulate_scenarios(data.frame(R0 = c(0.7, 0.9, 0.95), w = 0.3, k = 1))
fig2b <- fig2b |>
  mutate(R0lab = paste0("R0 = ", R0))

ggplot(fig2b, aes(nale)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = p_withdrawal, colour = R0lab), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = receptor_activation, colour = R0lab),
            linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Naloxone effect-site concentration (ng/mL)",
       y = "Withdrawal probability (solid) / receptor activation (dashed)",
       colour = NULL,
       title = "Figure 2b - withdrawal probability and receptor activation",
       caption = "Replicates Figure 2b of Dahan 2026 (w = 0.3).") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

# Withdrawal P50 shifts monotonically right with overdose severity.
p50 <- fig2b |>
  group_by(R0) |>
  summarise(c50 = crossing(nale, p_withdrawal, 0.5), .groups = "drop")
stopifnot(all(is.finite(p50$c50)), all(diff(p50$c50) > 0))
```

# Figure 3 - reversal, withdrawal and utility

Figure 3a shows the probability of respiratory reversal, the probability of
withdrawal, and their difference (the utility) at the reference overdose
severity `R0 = 0.9`, withdrawal threshold `w = 0.5`, and weight `k = 1`. Both
probabilities rise with naloxone concentration; their difference is positive
over a limited window and peaks near +0.2 (Dahan 2026 Results).

```{r figure-3a}
fig3a <- simulate_scenarios(data.frame(R0 = 0.9, w = 0.5, k = 1))

fig3a |>
  select(nale, p_reversal, p_withdrawal, utility) |>
  pivot_longer(-nale) |>
  ggplot(aes(nale, value, colour = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Naloxone effect-site concentration (ng/mL)", y = "Probability / utility",
       colour = NULL,
       title = "Figure 3a - reversal, withdrawal and utility (w = 0.5, R0 = 0.9)",
       caption = "Replicates Figure 3a of Dahan 2026.") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

# Peak utility near +0.2 (paper reports a positive peak of +0.2 at w = 0.5).
stopifnot(abs(max(fig3a$utility) - 0.2) < 0.08)
```

Figure 3b sweeps the withdrawal threshold. At `w = 0.3` the utility is negative
across roughly 10-30 ng/mL; at `w = 0.5` and `w = 0.7` it has positive peaks of
about +0.2 and +0.7 (Dahan 2026 Results). The Results text puts the negative
region at 10-30 ng/mL; the published Figure 3b, like the simulation below,
shows the `w = 0.3` utility clearly below zero from about 3 to 60 ng/mL with
its trough of about -0.42 near 10 ng/mL, so the text describes the core of the
dip rather than its full extent.

```{r figure-3b}
fig3b <- simulate_scenarios(data.frame(R0 = 0.9, w = c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7), k = 1))

ggplot(fig3b, aes(nale, utility, colour = factor(w))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Naloxone effect-site concentration (ng/mL)", y = "Utility",
       colour = "w",
       title = "Figure 3b - utility by withdrawal threshold (R0 = 0.9)",
       caption = "Replicates Figure 3b of Dahan 2026.")

peaks <- fig3b |>
  group_by(w) |>
  summarise(peak = utility[which.max(abs(utility))], .groups = "drop")
# Figure 3b extremes: trough about -0.42 at w = 0.3, peaks about +0.18 and
# +0.68 at w = 0.5 and 0.7. The C50 cohort is a fixed quantile grid, so the
# 0.05 tolerance covers only the coarse concentration grid.
stopifnot(
  abs(peaks$peak[peaks$w == 0.3] - (-0.42)) < 0.05,
  abs(peaks$peak[peaks$w == 0.5] - 0.18) < 0.05,
  abs(peaks$peak[peaks$w == 0.7] - 0.68) < 0.05
)
```

Figure 3c contrasts the opioid-tolerant subject (`w = 0.5`) with an
opioid-naive subject, for whom the probability of withdrawal is zero by
definition (Dahan 2026 Methods), so the utility reduces to the probability of
respiratory reversal.

```{r figure-3c}
fig3c <- bind_rows(
  fig3a |> transmute(nale, utility, group = "Individual with OUD, w = 0.5"),
  fig3a |> transmute(nale, utility = p_reversal,
                     group = "Opioid-naive individual, P(withdrawal) = 0")
)

ggplot(fig3c, aes(nale, utility, colour = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Naloxone effect-site concentration (ng/mL)", y = "Utility",
       colour = NULL,
       title = "Figure 3c - opioid-tolerant versus opioid-naive (R0 = 0.9)",
       caption = "Replicates Figure 3c of Dahan 2026.") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

# Figure 4 - influence of the withdrawal weight k

Increasing the weight `k` places greater numerical emphasis on avoiding
withdrawal without changing the probability of withdrawal itself; `k < 1`
prioritizes respiratory reversal.

```{r figure-4}
fig4 <- simulate_scenarios(data.frame(R0 = 0.9, w = 0.5, k = c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4)))

ggplot(fig4, aes(nale, utility, colour = factor(k))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Naloxone effect-site concentration (ng/mL)", y = "Utility",
       colour = "k",
       title = "Figure 4 - utility by withdrawal weight (w = 0.5, R0 = 0.9)",
       caption = "Replicates Figure 4 of Dahan 2026.")

# At 300 ng/mL every virtual subject is both reversed and in withdrawal, so the
# plateau utility is exactly 1 - k (Figure 4: 0.75 at k = 0.25, 0.50 at
# k = 0.5, 0 at k = 1). The C50 cohort is a fixed quantile grid, so this holds
# exactly on every machine.
hi <- fig4 |>
  group_by(k) |>
  summarise(u_hi = utility[which.max(nale)], .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(k)
stopifnot(all(abs(hi$u_hi - (1 - hi$k)) < 1e-8))
```

# Figure 5 - withdrawal versus intravenous naloxone dose

The withdrawal threshold was calibrated to `w = 0.30` against the proportion of
subjects with precipitated withdrawal after intravenous naloxone in an
emergency-department cohort (Yugar 2023) and in prospective studies in daily
opioid users (van Lemmen 2025b, 2026), with fitted baseline receptor
activations of about 0.90 and 0.96 (Dahan 2026 Discussion). Here the full
time course is simulated: a naloxone bolus enters `central`, reaches the effect
site with `ke0N`, and a subject counts as in withdrawal if Equation 6 is met at
any time in the next 4 h.

```{r figure-5}
dose_grid <- 10^seq(log10(0.02), log10(15), length.out = 40)
fig5_grid <- tidyr::expand_grid(R0 = c(0.90, 0.96), dose = dose_grid,
                                sid = seq_len(n_sub))
fig5_grid$id <- seq_len(nrow(fig5_grid))

fig5_ev <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  data.frame(id = fig5_grid$id, time = 0, evid = 1, amt = fig5_grid$dose,
             cmt = "central"),
  tidyr::expand_grid(id = fig5_grid$id, time = seq(1, 240, by = 1)) |>
    dplyr::mutate(evid = 0, amt = 0, cmt = "central")
) |>
  dplyr::arrange(id, time, dplyr::desc(evid))

fig5_sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(
  mod, fig5_ev,
  params = data.frame(id = fig5_grid$id, etalec50 = eta_grid[fig5_grid$sid],
                      rbase = fig5_grid$R0, wd_thres = 0.3),
  returnType = "data.frame"
)

fig5 <- fig5_sim |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(any_withdrawal = max(withdrawal), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(fig5_grid, by = "id") |>
  group_by(R0, dose) |>
  summarise(p_withdrawal = mean(any_withdrawal), .groups = "drop")

# Mean +/- 95% CI digitized from Figure 5 by the maintainers (the 7 mg Yugar
# point is drawn without a CI in the figure).
fig5_obs <- data.frame(
  source = c(rep("Yugar 2023", 3), rep("van Lemmen 2025b, 2026", 2)),
  dose = c(0.063, 0.9, 7, 2, 5),
  pct = c(12.5, 39, 100, 50, 80),
  lo = c(7, 29, NA, 26, 28.5),
  hi = c(20, 49.5, NA, 74, 100)
)

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = fig5, aes(dose, 100 * p_withdrawal,
                             linetype = paste0("R0 = ", R0)), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_errorbar(data = fig5_obs, aes(dose, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0.05,
                na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_point(data = fig5_obs, aes(dose, pct, shape = source), size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Intravenous naloxone dose (mg)",
       y = "Precipitated withdrawal (% of subjects)",
       linetype = NULL, shape = NULL,
       title = "Figure 5 - withdrawal versus naloxone dose (w = 0.3)",
       caption = "Replicates Figure 5 of Dahan 2026.") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

# The published curves reach 50% withdrawal at about 1.1 mg (R0 = 0.90, solid)
# and about 2.7 mg (R0 = 0.96, dashed), read from Figure 5.
ed50 <- fig5 |>
  group_by(R0) |>
  summarise(ed50 = crossing(dose, p_withdrawal, 0.5), .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(ed50, digits = 2,
             caption = "Simulated naloxone dose giving 50% withdrawal (mg).")
stopifnot(
  abs(ed50$ed50[ed50$R0 == 0.90] / 1.1 - 1) < 0.15,
  abs(ed50$ed50[ed50$R0 == 0.96] / 2.7 - 1) < 0.15
)
```

# Equation 8 - the utility crossover threshold w\*

The paper gives the withdrawal threshold at which the utility changes sign as
`w* = 1 - 0.5/R0` (Equation 8), with reported crossovers of 0.38 at `R0 = 0.8`,
0.44 at `R0 = 0.9`, and 0.47 at `R0 = 0.95`. Sweeping `w` at each severity and
finding where the peak utility crosses zero reproduces these values.

```{r equation-8}
w_sweep <- seq(0.30, 0.52, by = 0.01)
cross <- lapply(c(0.8, 0.9, 0.95), function(R0) {
  s <- simulate_scenarios(data.frame(R0 = R0, w = w_sweep, k = 1))
  peak <- s |>
    group_by(w) |>
    summarise(peak = utility[which.max(abs(utility))], .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(w)
  w_star <- crossing(peak$w, peak$peak, 0)
  data.frame(R0 = R0, w_star_sim = w_star, w_star_eq8 = 1 - 0.5 / R0)
}) |>
  bind_rows()

knitr::kable(cross, digits = 3,
             caption = "Simulated utility crossover w* vs Equation 8.")

# Equation 8 is an exact analytic identity (0.5 = (1 - w*) * R0). The
# Monte-Carlo crossover reproduces it to within ~0.02-0.03: near the crossover
# the peak utility is ~0, so the zero-crossing is sensitive to the finite
# (200-subject) cohort and the discrete concentration/threshold grids, biasing
# w* slightly low. A mis-transcribed C50, R0 relationship or withdrawal
# equation would move w* by far more than this tolerance. The crossover must
# also increase monotonically with overdose severity (Equation 8).
stopifnot(
  all(is.finite(cross$w_star_sim)),
  all(diff(cross$w_star_sim) > 0),
  all(abs(cross$w_star_sim - cross$w_star_eq8) < 0.03)
)
```

# Assumptions and deviations

- The paper simulated 40,000 subjects per scenario; for a fast, reproducible
  vignette the maintainers use 200 subjects per scenario on a deterministic
  log-normal C50 quantile grid (variance 0.31). Only C50 varies between
  subjects, matching the paper; all other parameters are fixed at typical
  values, so 200 subjects resolve the population probabilities to within a
  few percent.
- The C50 typical value is taken as 4.08 ng/mL from the Methods text and
  Figure 1; Table 1 rounds it to 4.1 ng/mL. The two differ by 0.5 %.
- The fentanyl effect-site concentration is held constant for each subject at
  the value giving the chosen overdose severity `R0` (Equation 4 rearranged);
  the model does not carry a fentanyl PK compartment, consistent with the
  paper's steady-state formulation.
- Overdose severity `R0`, withdrawal threshold `w`, and withdrawal weight `k`
  are shipped as fixed parameters at the paper's reference values
  (`R0 = 0.9`, `w = 0.3`, `k = 1`) and overridden per scenario in the figures
  above via `rxSolve(params = ...)`, matching the ranges in Table 1.
- The paper does not state how an intravenous naloxone dose was mapped to the
  withdrawal outcome in the Figure 5 calibration. The maintainers simulate a
  bolus through the model's own naloxone kinetics and count a subject as in
  withdrawal if Equation 6 is met at any time in the following 4 h, with the
  fitted overdose severities of about 0.90 and 0.96 (Discussion). This
  reproduces the 50% withdrawal doses of both published curves to within 15%.
  The literature data points in the Figure 5 plot are digitized by the
  maintainers from the published figure and are shown for orientation only.
- As of 2026-11-17 no correction notice is listed for this article.
